problem: State-of-the-art VLN agents on R2R (Speaker-Follower follower, Self-Monitoring) report large gains, but it is unclear which modality the gains come from. The paper shows these agents do not learn visual grounding that generalizes to unseen buildings: their ResNet image features can actually hurt performance in unseen environments.
motivation: If an agent can reach the goal without looking, success-rate gains do not mean better vision-language grounding. The key observation is that 'blind' versions of SF and SM, with visual features set to zero, match or beat their visual counterparts on val-unseen. Visual and non-visual agents also succeed on different episodes, so their errors are complementary. With only 61 training environments, low-level CNN features overfit to scene appearance, whereas symbolic object labels should transfer to new scenes.
key_idea: Split grounding into modality-specific experts that share one instruction encoder, one expert each for ResNet appearance, symbolic object detections and route structure only (no vision), then average their action logits.
insight: R2R's discrete connectivity graph lets much of the language ground into route geometry alone ('turn left' at the only possible turn). Non-visual agents therefore reach 35.2 SR (SF) and 39.7 SR (SM) on val-unseen, versus 29.0 and 40.5 with ResNet features. Symbolic object features (Faster R-CNN labels embedded with GloVe) generalize better than pixel CNN features: SF RN+Obj reaches 39.8 vs 29.0, and SM Obj reaches 41.6 vs 40.5. Mixing experts of different modalities beats ensembling same-modality agents: SM (RN, no vis.) gets 46.9, versus 43.5 for (RN, RN) and 41.0 for (no vis., no vis.). Adding the object expert raises this to 49.5, and joint training with a shared encoder reaches 51.9. A single RN+Obj model with the same inputs gets only 39.5, so the modality split itself acts as an inductive bias that forces grounding into each modality.
method: Non-visual ablation analysis: SF and SM agents are trained and tested with all visual feature vectors zeroed (teacher-forcing and student-forcing variants), leaving only route or action structure, and compared against ResNet-152 versions on R2R val-seen and val-unseen.

Object-based representation: a Faster R-CNN detector trained on Visual Genome provides the top-150 detections per viewpoint. Each detection becomes a vector: summed GloVe vectors of the object label and its attribute labels, concatenated with the bounding-box location.
Object attention: the same visual attention as SF/SM pools the object vectors into x_obj,att, which either replaces the ResNet attended feature ('Obj') or is concatenated with it ('RN+Obj').

Mixture-of-experts, separate training: independently trained agents with different modalities (RN, Obj, no vis.) are combined at every step by averaging action logits. Averaging logits worked slightly better than averaging probabilities.

Mixture-of-experts, joint training: a single agent has one shared LSTM instruction encoder and several modality-specific LSTM decoders. Each decoder is supervised with the ground-truth actions using the standard loss, and at test time the decoders' logits are averaged.

Evaluation protocol: no speaker data augmentation, greedy decoding (no beam search, pragmatic inference or progress-monitor search), SM reimplemented without the progress monitor, and the checkpoint selected on val-seen.

setting.backbone: LSTM seq2seq encoder-decoder agents: Speaker-Follower follower and a Self-Monitoring reimplementation without progress monitor, trained from scratch. Inputs are frozen pretrained features from ResNet-152 and from Faster R-CNN (Visual Genome) detections embedded with GloVe.
setting.training_data: R2R train split only (61 Matterport3D environments), with no speaker data augmentation. Uses a frozen ResNet-152 and a Faster R-CNN pretrained on Visual Genome as feature extractors.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (ResNet-152 features per orientation) + object detections (labels, attributes, boxes) per viewpoint
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (move to an adjacent connected viewpoint or stop)

numbers_note: Only success rate (SR) is reported; no SPL, NE, OSR or TL. No test-server results. The val-seen SR of the main joint-training model is not given; a footnote says only 'On the val-seen split, we maintain performance comparable to the original SM model.' Ensembles (Table 3) are reported on val-unseen only. All results use greedy decoding without data augmentation, so they are not directly comparable to the SF/SM papers' beam-search or augmented numbers.
results: Non-visual agents outperform or match their ResNet counterparts on R2R val-unseen: SF 35.2 vs 29.0 SR (teacher-forcing) and 31.7 vs 29.0 (student-forcing), SM 39.7 vs 40.5. Object representations improve generalization, e.g. SF RN+Obj reaches 39.8. The jointly trained 3-expert SM agent (RN, Obj, no vis.) reaches 51.9 SR on val-unseen, more than 10 points above the single-decoder CNN baselines (SF 29.0, SM 40.5). It also beats same-modality ensembles, e.g. SM (RN, RN) at 43.5.
limitations: Reports only success rate, on R2R validation splits only; no SPL, no test-server results, and no other datasets.

The analysis is restricted to greedy decoding without data augmentation, beam search or the progress monitor, so it is unclear how the gains carry over to full SF/SM pipelines. The SM model is a reimplementation.
Gains come partly from ensembling multiple decoders, which multiplies inference cost. The analysis is tied to R2R's discrete nav-graph, whose route structure enables the non-visual shortcut.
